strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length inputs is a meaningful and timely task, and the paper crisply distinguishes it from camera-controlled I2V and video-to-future-video paradigms (Fig. 2, Eq. 2-3).

The dual spatio-temporal conditioning idea is intuitive and well-executed: temporally adjacent frames for motion continuity plus projected static point-cloud views for spatial consistency, which elegantly resolves the tension between freezing dynamics and preserving static scene structure.

The three-stage dynamic masking pipeline (optical-flow thresholding -> CoTracker3 backward tracking -> SAM2 propagation) is a thoughtful, practical solution to ghosting artifacts in dynamic scenes, and the ablation (Tab. 4) confirms it is a major contributor (~0.8dB PSNR drop without it).

Comprehensive evaluation covering four axes: scene/spatial consistency (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on revisited viewpoints), geometric consistency (MEt3R), camera controllability (mRotErr/mTransErr/mCamMC), and video quality (FVD + VBench++), with consistent improvements over DFoT and strong camera-control baselines (e.g., 77% MEt3R reduction, best FVD of 127.5).

Leverages pretrained priors (CogVideoX) with minimal architectural changes (channel-concat conditioning), keeping training cheap (4K iterations, 4 H100s) and preserving generation quality - a sensible and efficient design choice.
Good related-work positioning against Gen3C, StaRGen, DFoT, and camera-control methods, clearly articulating why prior geometry-conditioned work does not address dynamics beyond temporal boundaries.
weaknesses: Limited novelty depth: the framework is largely a careful assembly of off-the-shelf components (MegaSLAM, SAM2, CoTracker3, RAFT/FlowD, CogVideoX) with channel-concat conditioning; the 'dual conditioning' insight is sensible but the technical machinery is engineering-heavy rather than conceptually new.

Missing key baseline: the paper argues that directly conditioning on retrieved raw frames from earlier in the video would 'freeze out' dynamics, but never empirically tests this alternative. A baseline that retrieves T raw spatially-adjacent frames (without 3D memory/masking) is needed to isolate the benefit of the 3D scene memory itself.

Unfair comparison setup in the camera-controllability evaluation: baselines (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FLoVD, AC3D) condition on a single image, while the proposed method receives 9 temporal frames plus spatially projected views - substantially more conditioning information. No baseline is given equivalent access (e.g., a multi-frame-conditioned model), so camera-control gains are confounded.

Scene-consistency comparison is thin: only DFoT is evaluated quantitatively (Tab. 1) despite Gen3C and StaRGen being discussed as closely related; missing ablations such as replacing the point-cloud projection with a lightweight geometric representation, or ablating the temporal window w.

The camera-control mechanism is implicit (control arises from warped static views rather than an explicit trajectory encoder). There is no analysis of robustness to large viewpoint changes, novel regions not covered by any input frame, or failure cases when SLAM/masking fails; qualitative figures (Fig. 6, 7) are cherry-picked, and no user study is provided.

Potential evaluation/data concerns: training on OpenVid-1M and evaluating FVD/VBench++ on DynPose-100K raises possible distribution or contamination questions that are not discussed; the protocol for matching 'same viewpoint' frames for PSNR/SSIM is only sketched and could favor the proposed method.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, the fine-tuning dataset mix and filtering details are vague (only L>100, sources named), and several implementation specifics (projection resolution, handling of invalid/unprojected regions in warped views, τ threshold) are unspecified.

Presentation issues: notation inconsistencies (Eq. 9 reuses C_i ambiguously, P^(n)_static vs P_static), some overclaiming in the abstract/intro ('significantly outperforms' based on one main quantitative competitor for scene consistency), and no discussion of limitations or failure modes.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and well-motivated problem—scene-consistent, camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length inputs—that existing camera-control (single-image conditioning) and video-to-future-video (short temporal window) methods do not handle well.

The dual spatio-temporal conditioning idea (temporal frames for motion continuity + projected static point clouds for spatial consistency) is clearly articulated, and the dynamic masking pipeline (optical flow residual + CoTracker3 backward tracking + SAM2 propagation) is a sensible and well-illustrated solution to ghosting artifacts in the 3D scene memory.
The method reuses a pretrained backbone (CogVideoX) with minimal architectural changes, preserving generative priors; training cost is modest and implementation details are reported.

Quantitative evaluations span multiple axes (spatial/geometric consistency, camera controllability, FVD, VBench++), and ablations cover both the number of spatial views and the necessity of dynamic masking, showing clear degradation without it.
Related work is well-organized and the distinctions from DFoT, Gen3C, and Stargen are clearly stated.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the framework is largely an assembly of off-the-shelf components (MegaSAM for poses/geometry, RAFT/FlowD for flow, CoTracker3 for tracking, SAM2 for segmentation, CogVideoX for generation) connected by channel-wise latent concatenation. The core 'contribution' is a conditioning recipe rather than a new modeling insight, and closely related works (Gen3C, ReCamMaster, Vid-Camedit, Stargen) already combine 3D lifting with video diffusion.

The main-task (scene-consistent generation) comparison includes only a single baseline, DFoT. Notably absent are Gen3C and ReCamMaster, which per the related-work section are the most architecturally relevant competitors. The camera-controllability baseline table (Table 2) compares against single-image I2V methods that do not receive the input video, so those comparisons are inherently unfair and overstate the advantage.

Evaluation protocol concerns: PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS are computed against generated trajectories revisiting input viewpoints, but the ground-truth 'future' frames for revisited viewpoints come from the input video itself, and the camera trajectories used for evaluation appear to be derived/selected favorably for the proposed method. There is no user study, no error-bar/statistical analysis, and no evaluation on truly out-of-distribution or very long (L >> 100) inputs despite the 'arbitrary-length' claim.

Training appears insufficient: only 4K iterations at batch size 8, with unclear data scale (how many videos from OpenVid-1M?). This raises questions about whether reported gains are robust or reflect a lightly-tuned setup; no convergence analysis or larger-scale fine-tuning comparison is provided.

Robustness of the pipeline is unexamined: the method depends critically on SLAM pose/depth quality (MegaSAM), flow-based dynamic detection thresholds (fixed τ), and FOV-overlap-based retrieval. There is no failure-case analysis, no discussion of static objects that later move (acknowledged as a limitation but not measured), and no quantitative evaluation of mask quality itself.

Several claims are unsupported or overstated: 'significant computational efficiency' is asserted but no runtime/memory comparison is given; the 'surprising' camera-control benefit of the 3D memory is claimed without isolating it in an ablation (the ablation only varies n and the dynamic mask, not temporal-vs-spatial conditioning in isolation).

Writing issues: the paper is repetitive (the dual conditioning motivation is restated many times across Sections 1–3), equations are largely trivial restatements of the pipeline, and no code or project page is promised, weakening reproducibility.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: scene-consistent, camera-controllable generation from arbitrary-length inputs, which is a real gap between camera-controllable (I2V-based) and video-to-future-video methods.

The dual spatio-temporal conditioning idea is sensible and elegant: using static-only 3D scene memory as a spatial prompt resolves the tension between referencing distant frames and letting dynamic content evolve naturally.

The three-stage dynamic masking pipeline (optical-flow residual detection -> backward tracking with CoTracker3 -> SAM2 propagation) is a practical, well-designed contribution to avoid ghosting artifacts in dynamic scenes.

Comprehensive evaluation across four axes (camera controllability, video quality, spatial consistency, geometric consistency) with consistent improvements over strong baselines (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FLoVD, AC3D, DFoT), plus ablations on n and dynamic masking that support the design choices.
The approach preserves pretrained priors by reusing the conditioning channel rather than building a bespoke architecture, making it computationally practical and easy to adopt.
weaknesses: Limited baseline coverage for the core task: DFoT is essentially the only direct competitor for scene-consistent generation; stronger recent long-horizon methods (e.g., Stargen, Gen3C variants) are discussed but not empirically compared.

Heavy dependence on a cascade of off-the-shelf components (MegaSLAM/MegaSAM, RAFT/SeaRAFT, CoTracker3, SAM2); error propagation from these modules at inference time (e.g., SLAM failures on hard videos) is not analyzed or stress-tested, and robustness/failure cases are not shown.

Quantitative gains over the closest baseline (DFoT) on several metrics are relatively modest, and FVD/VBench++ comparisons favor the proposed method partly because it conditions on more ground-truth input frames than baselines designed for single-image conditioning, raising fairness questions about the comparison protocol.

Evaluation is confined to two datasets (RealEstate10K, DynPose-100K) and 1,000 videos each; no user study is provided to support perceptual claims about consistency and motion realism, which matter greatly for this task.

Training is small-scale (4K iterations, 4 H100s) and reproducibility details are thin: no mention of code/model release, and some design choices (threshold tau, camera-conditioning-free claim vs. implicit trajectory leakage through projections) are not fully ablated.

The claim that precise camera control arises 'without any other explicit camera conditioning' is interesting but under-validated; it is unclear how well the method handles novel trajectories that deviate substantially from the input video's coverage.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined new task: scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length input videos, articulating the static-vs-dynamic consistency tension precisely.

Clean architectural insight: the dual spatio-temporal conditioning reuses frozen pretrained priors (CogVideoX) by repurposing the image-conditioning channel for concatenated spatial prompts, avoiding auxiliary architectures or ControlNet-style blocks.

The dynamic masking pipeline (optical-flow differencing, backward point tracking with CoTracker3, SAM2 propagation) is a sensible and non-trivial solution to ghosting artifacts in static point-cloud extraction, and is well illustrated (Figs. 4-5).

Extensive ablations in the appendix: stage-wise masking ablation (Tab. 6), temporal window size w (Tab. 7), number of projected views n (Tab. 8), swapping MegaSAM for DepthAnything v3 (Tab. 9), inference-time analysis (Tab. 10), and long-video generation on DAVIS (Tab. 5) with three adapted baseline strategies.

Evaluation covers four axes (camera controllability, video quality, scene consistency, geometric consistency) with standard metrics (mRotErr/mTransErr, FVD, VBench++, MEt3R, PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), and the method consistently outperforms DFoT on the consistency task and existing camera-control methods on controllability/quality.
Good discussion of limitations (SLAM overhead, mask quality dependence) and positioning against concurrent works (SPMem, WorldMem, Gen3C); reproducibility statement with code release promised.
weaknesses: The main spatial-consistency comparison (Tab. 1) has only a single direct baseline (DFoT). While the authors argue no prior work directly addresses the task, the single-comparison setup weakens the headline claim of 'significantly outperforms existing methods' for scene consistency; DFoT's failure is attributed to a memory constraint that is somewhat known a priori.

Absolute PSNR/SSIM values are very low (e.g., ~13 dB PSNR, ~0.37 SSIM on DynPose-100K), making it hard to judge whether the reported improvements (PSNR gains under 1 dB in some ablations) reflect meaningful perceptual consistency; pixel-space PSNR between generated and ground-truth future frames is a noisy proxy.

Potential evaluation/conditioning advantage concern: the model conditions on projected views of the ground-truth-derived point cloud of the same scene during both training and evaluation, giving it scene-specific geometric information that image- or trajectory-conditioned baselines (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D) never receive; the comparison in Tab. 2/3 is thus between systems with very different information access, and the paper does not disentangle this.

Camera-control evaluation protocol adapts an I2V setting (single image + trajectory) to a framework that also ingests the full input video and its SLAM reconstruction; fairness of comparing mRotErr/mTransErr across these mismatched conditionings deserves more scrutiny.

Temporal error accumulation in autoregressive long-video extension is acknowledged but not addressed, limiting the practical claim of 'arbitrary-length' generation; no long-video quantitative comparison against SPMem or Gen3C-style methods.

The dynamic masking pipeline depends on several external models (SEA-RAFT, CoTracker3, SAM2, MegaSAM/VGGT) with hyperparameters (threshold τ, sampling density) not fully specified; robustness of the pipeline to SLAM failure or heavily dynamic scenes is not quantified.

Novelty is moderate: the core idea (project static 3D reconstruction as conditioning for camera-controllable video diffusion) is closely related to Gen3C, SPMem, and ViD-CamEdit; the contribution is primarily the static-only separation and efficient conditioning, which should be stated more carefully against these works.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly motivated and practically important task (scene-consistent, camera-controllable video continuation from arbitrary-length input), and the dual spatio-temporal conditioning idea is intuitive and well-articulated.

The technical pipeline is complete and modular: dynamic SLAM, a three-stage dynamic masking strategy (flow thresholding, backward point tracking, SAM2 propagation), and point-cloud rendering as spatial prompts, all described with enough detail to follow.

The experimental section is unusually thorough for this area: it includes comparisons along four axes (camera controllability, video quality, scene consistency, geometric consistency), ablations of nearly every component (dynamic mask stages, n, w, choice of 3D reconstruction module), long-video generation results on DAVIS, and inference-time analysis.

The ablation on spatial prompts (n=0 baseline) convincingly demonstrates that the projected 3D conditioning is the key driver of both scene consistency and camera controllability, and the component-swap experiment (MegaSAM vs. DepthAnything v3) supports the claimed modularity.
Reproducibility is supported by a clear statement, training details (4K iterations, 4 H100s), dataset curation description, and a commitment to release code.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework is largely an assembly of existing off-the-shelf components (MegaSAM, SEA-RAFT, CoTracker3, SAM2, CogVideoX-I2V) with a channel-concatenation conditioning trick and no new architecture or training objective. The main contribution is system integration, which may not meet the novelty bar of a top-tier venue.

Potential circularity in the scene-consistency evaluation: the spatial conditioning is a rendering of the static point cloud from exactly the target viewpoint, so PSNR/SSIM on revisited trajectories may substantially reflect the model copying its (near ground-truth) conditioning rather than learned long-range consistency. This confound is not analyzed or ablated (e.g., by measuring how much of the generated content is copied verbatim from the spatial prompt).

Baseline comparisons are of questionable fairness: camera-controllable baselines (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D) are I2V/T2V models that never see the input video, while this method is effectively given a warped rendering of the target static scene. The headline camera-control and FVD advantages may stem primarily from this extra information rather than a better control mechanism.

The single most comparable baseline for the core claim (DFoT) is only compared on two datasets, and DFoT is not originally a camera-controllable method; the closest related systems (Gen3C, SPMem) are not compared quantitatively due to code unavailability, so the central claim of 'significantly outperforms existing methods' rests on a thin set of direct comparisons.

Absolute generation quality metrics remain low (e.g., ~13 PSNR, ~0.37 SSIM on DynPose-100K), and there is no human/user study to validate perceptual quality, which is standard for video generation papers.

Robustness of the pipeline is under-characterized: the method depends on SLAM pose estimation and dynamic masking quality, but failure cases (SLAM drift, segmentation errors propagating into conditioning, highly dynamic or egocentric footage) are not quantified, and the training set curation (only 50K curated clips, filtering of 'excessive camera motion') may bias evaluation toward favorable conditions.

Several important design details are underspecified: how viewpoint similarity / field-of-view overlap is computed for retrieval, how occluded/unobserved regions in projections are handled, and the sensitivity of the threshold tau in the flow-based mask.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper defines 'scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation' and clearly articulates why existing single-image camera-control methods and short-window video-to-future-video methods (e.g., Cosmos-predict-2) are insufficient, particularly regarding revisit consistency and handling of dynamic vs. static content.

The core idea is sensible and well-executed: dual spatio-temporal conditioning with a static-only 3D scene memory, where the dynamic masking is critical because naively warping frames with moving objects would inject stale dynamic content into the future. The distinction between temporal conditioning (last frames) and spatial conditioning (static point cloud projections) is clean and well justified.

The three-stage dynamic masking pipeline (optical-flow thresholding, backward point tracking with CoTracker3, SAM2 propagation) addresses a real failure mode (ghosting artifacts), and Fig. 4 plus the stage-wise ablation in Table 6 convincingly demonstrate that each stage contributes.

Comprehensive evaluation across four aspects (scene consistency, camera controllability, video quality, geometric consistency) with appropriate metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on revisited viewpoints, MEt3R, camera error metrics, FVD, VBench++), and a substantial set of ablations (n, w, dynamic mask stages, SLAM backbone swap, inference time).

The architecture is minimally invasive: repurposing CogVideoX-I2V-5B's image conditioning channel via channel-wise latent concatenation keeps the pretrained DiT intact, and the appendix shows the SLAM component is swappable (DepthAnything v3 improves results and latency), evidencing a modular, future-proof design.

The long-video generation experiments (Table 5, DAVIS) with adapted baselines are a valuable addition beyond the main setting, and limitations (autoregressive error accumulation, SLAM overhead) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness concerns: the primary scene-consistency evaluation compares against DFoT, which conditions on a limited frame budget, while 3DScenePrompt receives rendered static point clouds projected at the exact target viewpoints being scored. Since the spatial prompt contains near-duplicate static content of the evaluation viewpoints (the trajectories deliberately revisit input viewpoints), PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS improvements are partly a consequence of the conditioning containing the answer, and gains over a purely memory-limited baseline like DFoT may be overstated. A baseline that retrieves and provides the actual source frames (upper bound for temporal conditioning) or a DFoT variant with comparable conditioning budget would strengthen claims.

The 'arbitrary-length input' claim has caveats: spatial retrieval depends on viewpoint similarity via estimated poses, which is only tested on datasets with well-conditioned camera motion (RealEstate10K, DynPose-100K); robustness on unconstrained casual video with SLAM failures is unexplored, and error propagation in iterative long-video generation is acknowledged but not solved.

The pipeline is heavily assembled from pretrained components (SEA-RAFT, SAM2, CoTracker3, MegaSAM/VGGT, CogVideoX), so the learned contribution is a relatively small fine-tuning step (4K iterations, 48 hours); this is efficient but limits the depth of the technical contribution relative to works with more substantive architectural or training innovations, and the concurrent SPMem (Wu et al., 2025) weakens novelty claims.

The dynamic masking ablation in Table 6 is internally inconsistent: MEt3R worsens from (a) 0.1040 to (b) 0.1556 and (c) 0.1576 before improving at (d), which the text does not explain; the metric trajectory suggests either measurement noise on a subset or that the claimed monotonic benefit of each stage does not hold uniformly.

Camera controllability gains over DFoT are marginal (2.38 vs 2.40 mRotErr), and the main differentiator over strong recent baselines (AC3D, CameraCtrl2, Gen3C) is confined to the revisit-consistency setting; Table 3 comparisons mix models with different backbones and training scales, complicating attribution of quality gains to the proposed conditioning.

Metric details are thin in places: how the top-n spatially adjacent frames and field-of-view overlap are computed, the effect of the L1 threshold τ, and evaluation-set construction (e.g., how the 1,000-video subsets and revisit trajectories were generated) are underspecified, which slightly hampers reproducibility despite the stated code release promise.
